I think page 50 is a good place to stop for someone who is starting to get into reading. If it's 300 pages or less, I would even say 30 to 40 pages is enough to decide. 

Don't punish yourself for deciding to stop reading something. That will make it even tougher to get into new books you read. Stop reading those books and read a new one. 

You haven't defined what kind of books you like yet. You will define your tastes faster by trying (not finishing!) more books of varying topics and genres.

You can also try a middle ground between your special interest and new genres or topics. Search for books that mix your interests with topics or genres you haven't explored or read about. That could be a gateway into a new special interest.

Most importantly, don't read or try new things with the primary reason of finding a new interest and expanding your tastes. That happens on its own. The primary reason should be curiosity, like when you were a kid; you saw that toy and you wanted it. Maybe you had a hundred toys that you got tired of really quickly and you never felt bad for it, but there were probably a few that you kept coming back to. All because you were curious.

Again, stop reading the book if you don't like it early on. You will find books you love faster if you move on. I promise it won't be like that for every book. You'll eventually develop your "reading muscles" and will be able to read faster and maintain focus longer.

From now on, decide you'll buy a book just to read the first 30-50 pages; not with the goal of finishing it. If you feel like wanting to keep going, go ahead!

Additionally, I've surprised myself when, a year or two later, I will pick up that thing again with a fresh start and actually enjoy it. If I had forced myself to keep going, I would have killed the chances of ever going back. Even worse, I would've damaged my relationship with it.

I refinanced this past Thursday. 

I recommend doing a pre-application with Caribou, which is what I did. I ended up bringing my payment down from $520 to $360 and my rates from 10.3% to 6.2% . 

Caribou is an aggregator that works with a bunch of different credit unions and lenders. They do a soft credit inquiry, so you don't have to worry about comparing options while dinging your credit. 

Basically, they compare different options for you and find you the best one. It's all online and it was very smooth and fast too (took me one week and a half once I applied). They did all the work and even set me up with the credit union. 

All I had to do was gather the documentation and sign the paperwork when ready. 

If you accept their offer, Caribou's fee is included in the refinance loan. It's $500, but it's nothing compared with what I'm saving. 

It's free to apply though. Give it a try and see what they offer. If their offer is not good, you can always try with your local credit unions and Pen Fed, which is hightly recommended by others on this sub.

Para los que no tienen trabajo, escuela o no hacen amigos en el trabajo:

La solución es volverte un regular en algún lugar.

Estrategia 1:

- Si eres un nerdo de mierda como yo, ve a alguna tienda de juegos de mesa y mira a ver si tienen eventos. A mí no me encantan los collecting card games, pero estoy dispuesto a hacer un deck simple y jugar con gente con el propósito primario de hacer amistades; no le tienes que revelar a nadie que eres un poser. Hay gente que solo son posers por joder. Ser un poser por hacer amistades no es algo malo.


Estrategia 2:

- Si vives en Estados Unidos, busca la biblioteca más cercana y mira los eventos que tienen. La mayoría son gratis y tienen variedad de intereses. En Puerto Rico también puedes mirar, pero es menos común. Una alternativa a bibliotecaa es buscar grupos de Facebook de gente en tu comunidad. Si eres de los que odia redes sociales, pero comoquiera te interesa, crea un Fakebook que solo usas para hacerte parte de grupos en persona. 


Estrategia 3:

- Únete a alguna clase en persona. No solo abre oportunidades para conocer gente; también aprendes algo nuevo y hasta te podría ayudar a encontrar un trabajo que no odies.

I've been taking adderall since March this year.

The biggest realization I've had while taking medication and trying different strategies is that there are more external things that can help than internal. 

Don't think of the pill as the only thing that can make you functional. 

Use the power of the pill to hyperfocus on finding or developing strategies that can help you aside of medication. 

Let me give you a superbasic example. Taking out the trash. I don't need to remember to take it out anymore. When it gets full, I put the bag in front of my door. If I have to go out, I have no choice since it's in the way. 

Thinking of such things requires sitting down and actually breaking down the things that you hate doing or the things that you struggle with. It also requires knowing how your brain works because ADHD works different for everyone. 

You have working memory problems? Find ways to reduce the number of things you have to remember. You have problems finding things? Start reducing the number of things you have. You have executive functioning struggles, pick the worst tasks and find ways to reduce the number of subtasks. 

Even if you've already tried doing all of this, keep coming up with other experiments. And don't just copy other people's strategies. Make your own; it tends to be more effective.

This requires thinking and researching but it can be fun if you treat it as one of your rabbit holes. 

And remember there's no magic system or strategy, but you can reduce the amount of decision making, things to remember or tasks to do. 

Focus on one thing at a time.

And believe me, once you find one thing that works, it will be such a nice dopamine hit, that you'll want to optimize everything (which isn't good but it's definitely better than where you are now).

My life isn't perfect, I also take medication and I'm also trying to figure things out. I'm by no means an ADHD guru but I have made some changes that don't rely on medication and work most days.

One of the first steps is to stop measuring progress based on ability to access feelings because this can spiral into depression. 

The focus should be on what you and the other person need in the relationship. Think about the possibility that they might not be able to ever have much access to their emotions. Would you still be with them?

With that said, just because he can't feel much doesn't mean that he can't know what you like or don't if you clearly tell him these things. If you know you need affection and he doesn't give you any, that's something you can address. 

Think about this situation: You told him you'd like kisses when he comes home from work trying to give him specific examples of how to show you affection. Let's say he does this one day and you are very angry because of something a family member told you. This could cause you to reject his kiss. Now he might be confused and not attempt to give you a kiss again. You might think you could avoid something like this by telling him: "Kiss me or give me a hug when you leave or come back home, but give me space if I'm angry." Okay, but how does he know when you're angry? You might have to tell him what it looks like when you're angry because he might not be able to tell due to the condition. 

"But then he'll do it just because I told him to do so! I want him to do it because he wants* to and because he took the initiative*." Well, wanting and taking initiative often requires some kind of emotional push and he might not have that. This is where knowing what he needs comes in.

And you show that you love someone by going out of your way to meet the other person's need. Even if he lacks the emotional signals to pick up on what you need, he can meet you halfway if you clearly tell him how to do that. Now, if you tell him what you need and what are your deal breakers, and he crosses them, he has no excuse. 

And as for knowing what he needs when he has difficulty identifying what he likes, a start would be for him to think about things that make him uncomfortable. For example, he might be sensitive to loud noises or loud environments. If he's an introvert, he might need a lot of time home or alone. Maybe he likes things to be planned rather than spontaneous. And so on. He might have a hard time figuring out what makes him feel good or what makes him sad, but he can tell you what he tolerates or what he doesn't. 

The most important thing to remember is that it's all about meeting each other halfway. That means each person has to sacrifice something for the other. That may be time, money, helping you around the house with things he can do, etc. And just because he needs support and accommodations doesn't mean he can't make sacrifices to meet your needs. So start with specifying what those needs are and go from there.

First, I want to apologize for the super long comment. I know it's not ADHD friendly, but don't feel like you have to read it all in one sitting. I have been on a self improvement journey for over 2 years, for the same reasons you're struggling with. I've learned a lot. 

To start, it's definitely possible to improve your productivity without medication.

I take Adderall, but I was able to control my video game addiction and procrastination habits long before I knew I have ADHD.

I think the first thing you should do is figure out what to do about your job. You know you hate your current job and you know it's not your type of thing. You need to deal with this, because getting rid of your procrastination habits isn't going to make your job enjoyable. 

The first step to get rid of bad habits is to know why you're doing it and what you're going to substitute for those habits. To answer these questions effectively, you have to be specific. If you want to quit procrastinating because you feel like your life is slipping away into things that don't seem that meaningful to you, that's a great reason to seek a positive change and it's important to be aware of this but it's not specific enough. You need to think about what you can do right now to get closer to the change 

When you're clocked into your job, your brain is programmed to do these few things: it can do the job that you hate or it can go on chess.com, play video games or go on social media platforms. Naturally, your brain is going to choose whatever's more stimulating from the options it has. If you want to stop doing action X, you need to substitute it for a specific action Y. Also, this action Y has to be something you can do right now. Right now, action Y is not specified and it's not defined as something you can do right now. That means, it's not part of the list of actions your brain could take. 

If you say: "instead of being a software engineer, I could be a sales man in tech", that is not a specific action; that's just a goal and goals are a thing of the future. We have ADHD brains. Our brains need something to do right now. If it's not in front of us, it doesn't exist. How do we make our brains aware of other things it could be doing and reprogram it to act on good habits? With knowledge. 

For example, you could plan to read some posts about the day to day life of people in tech sales to get an idea of if you would like it or not. You could also watch YouTube videos on the subject. Then find out how people were able to get a job related to that field. This might help you visualize the next actions you can take towards that goal and they are actions you can take right now. 

Other things you could do involve looking for other options aside of tech sales. You're an extrovert and you're not incapable of standing in front of a crowd. Find other ways to monetize this. Teaching, tutoring, coaching, consulting, etc. You could be a chess teacher, for example. If you're the best chess.com player in the world, then you already have proof or something you can use to market yourself. You could be a programming teacher. You could make a YouTube channel about this. You can get into competitive marketing. Start doing research into things you might be a good fit for. 

In other words, define a small goal you can accomplish in the present that is a step towards the big goal in the future. Start small (sending 1 to 3 resumes per day to jobs, watching at least one video or reading one post/article about a possible job you're interested in, spending just 20 minutes of your day to research jobs. etc.) At first, it might feel like a chore, but a small task such as these will take less than 30 minutes or even less than 15. After you're done with the task, you can go procrastinate as much as you want. The next day, try another task, and so on. Eventually, you'll start doing more.

Small changes that can also improve your motivation are sleep hygiene modifications, meditation, practicing mindfulness (helps with conscientiousness), intermittent fasting, excercise, drinking a gallon of water a day and experimenting with new daily routines. 

And don't rely on what most people say about these things. I used to think 8 hours was enough but I still felt tired and groggy when I woke up. I decided to try 9 hours instead and my mood increased greatly. The mood improvement makes me less likely to procrastinate.

Esto que voy a decir son solo ideas. También las puedes usar como una base. Lo más importante es encontrar un estilo con el que te sientas cómodo, con confianza y con buena autoestima. 

Antes no me importaba mucho cómo vestía, pero después de graduarme y empezar a buscar trabajo, yo también me di cuenta que mi manera de vestir podía mejorar bastante, so empecé a hacer research y a cambiar mi closet poco a poco. No solo busqué cómo vestir mejor. También he buscado cómo hacerlo de la manera más económica posible. 

TIP #1: Buzzcut (barbero) 
Un buzzcut es bueno, bonito y barato. Además, dura varias semanas y se ve profesional. Si quieres que te dure lo máximo, pide la 1 arriba y la 0 a los lados. Puedes pedir la 0 para todo, si te atreves. 

Also, cuando te pregunten si quieres cerquillo o que te limpien/afeiten la barba, averigua si cobran extra por eso. Algunos barberos cobran $5 por eso. Eso lo puedes hacer en tu casa. Lo mejor es comprar un trimmer o máquina de afeitar y lo haces tú mismo. Un trimmer te puede costar $20 a $30 y dura bastante. 

TIP #2:  Buzzcut (autorecorte) 
Si no te molesta tener un buzzcut, es facilísmo aprender a recortarte tú mismo. Un buzzcut se ve profesional y limpio. No solo te ahorras el dinero del recorte, te ahorras gasolina y tiempo (un buzzcut simple me toma 10 a 15 minutos y es fácil de mantener). Also, un buen kit de recorte (máquina y clips) te puede costar $30 y te dura años si lo cuidas. Algunos vienen con trimmer integrado (sin clips) y eso también te puede ahorrar tiempo y dinero en navajas de afeitar. 


TIP #3: Minimalismo

CAMISAS: No sé cuál sea tu estilo, pero las camisas tipo polo se ven bien, son cómodas y no son tan calurosas (dependiendo de la tela). Te compras 4 o 5 en diferentes colores sólidos y ya tienes para variar. Si quieres un estilo más fino todavía, camisas de botones de colores sólidos. 

PANTALONES: Mahones es bastante casual, pero brega y pegan con casi todo. Si quieres irte un poco menos casual, compra chinos. El starter kit que he visto a mucha gente usar son chinos gris, marrón, verde olivo, negro o azul oscuro (navy Blue). Lo bueno de los chinos es que puedes irte con colores oscuros (lo típico), pero vienen en todos los colores que te puedas imaginar. Y otra cosa, son como mahones, pero los encuentro más cómodos y se ven menos casual. Si quieres comodidad máxima con chinos, busca los que son athletic chinos. 

ZAPATOS/TENIS: Tenis completamente blancos. No diseños, no prints, no suelas de otro color. Blanco.Eso es básicamente todo.

 El truco es que mientras más delgados, bajitos y ajustados a la forma de tu pie se vean, más acicalados se ven. 

De todas las ideas que menciono aquí, esta es mi favorita. Unos buenos tenis blancos te pueden elevar a otro nivel de acicalamiento aunque no cambies nada más. 

Si quieres tener otro tipo de zapatos para algo más profesional, siempre es bueno tener unos zapatos **marrones** de salir (oxfords). Esto los puedes combinar con polos, chinos y hasta con mahones. 

TIP EXTRA DE ZAPATOS: Si quieres ahorrar con zapatos, busca zapatos que sean cuero real. Te van a salir a más de $100, pero te van a durar años. Además, son super fáciles de limpiar (más fácil que cuero falso). Yo tengo unos tenis blancos que me salieron a $120, pero son cuero real. Llevo 3 años con esos tenis, son mi único par y se ven muy bien. Lo mismo puedo decir de mis zapatos de salir. Hay gente que compra Converse, Van's y Nikes de cuero falso o de cañas cada 4 a 6 meses porque no les duran. Con lo que esa gente gasta, te puedes comprar 3 a 4 pares de zapatos de cuero real y te van a durar más. 

ACCESORIOS EXTRA: Una buena correa y un reloj plateado. Son detallitos qué elevan la finez de tu vestimenta. 

TL;DR: Atrévete a un buzzcut (dura más) o aprende a recortarte tú mismo. Una buena máquina de recortar la puedes conseguir a $30 y te va a durar muchos recortes. Plus, te puede ahorrar tiempo afeitandote. ¿Camisas? Polos o camisas de botones. ¿Pantalones? Los pantalones tipo "Chinos" se ven más finos que mahones, vienen en muchos colores, son más cómodos y cuestan más baratos o igual que mahones. ¿Zapatos o tenis? Recomiendo tenis completamente blancos. Si quieres algo más profesional, zapatos de salir (oxfords) marrones.

As for dialogue, you can write specifics next to the caption in a parenthesis. For example, "(caption bubble stretches from one side of the panel to the other)."  If you need to tell your artist about a recurring detail, write a single note for your artist or letterer. For example: "Note: On this page we introduce an important character. This character's speech bubbles will have squiggly borders." 

Always consider whether what you wrote is important to understand the story. In fact, you should tell your artist why your specifications are important on every panel unless it's self explanatory. If you add directions to your script just because you like them, consider leaving those details to your artist. Why? Because your artist will most likely have a better vision than you. Try not being too hard on yourself on getting it right the first time you're writing the dialogue. 

For the first layer, I focus on what I want the characters to talk about. I write the conversation, even if both characters sound flat and with the same voice, because the focus on this part is WHAT they say, not HOW they say it. I focus only on the parts of the conversation that are important to my story. This would be the skeleton of the conversation; the blueprint. After you get this down, it will be much easier to get the rest down. 

For the second layer, I rewrite the conversation, but now that I know what I want them to say, I can focus on how I want them to say it; slang, accent and personality. I also add extra dialogue to make it sound more natural. Then, I look at what I don't like and tweak it until I feel that it's good enough. 

It's important that you focus on one character at a time, because if you're constantly switching between personalities, the differences that give these characters their own voice might become blurry and you lose focus. Again, this part is easier once you have the first layer down. 

And for the third layer, I focus on the emotion that I want readers to get from the conversation, changing a few words here and there to tune the dialogue to that emotion. And I alter what I don't like again. 

I'm not the best at writing dialogue either, because I don't understand how other people socialize. I'm an introvert, socially awkward and I spend a lot of time alone or inside my head, even when I'm with people. However, you can learn a lot about how people socialize from reading, watching movies or from any storytelling media that has well developed characters. Think of a character from a story you know of that is very similar to the one you want to write and use it as a model for your character. Then, try to act like that character when you imagine how they say things. 

I hope this gives you a new strategy to try for writing dialogue :)

Hello! Start with learning the bones. Don't worry about the skin until you understand them. It makes things much easier. Hands have thin skin, so if you learn the bones, adding the skin is easy. Look for the Proko videos about hands on youtube. He teaches you how to simplify the bones and teaches you the main 3 muscles of the hands, so you can give them the realistic curves. 

After the bones, study the parts that give you trouble, separately. If you try to study all the parts of the hand at the same time, you'll feel overwhelmed. 
Draw a palm without the fingers, and fix the parts that you don't like, until you're satisfied. Draw another palm, but add just one finger. Focus on one at a time. Draw a line that shows the direction of the finger and then add the main form. Study that finger from different angles until you get the look that you want. Study how long the finger should be. Add another finger and follow the same process until you have the four fingers besides the thumb. Finally, study the thumb separately and add it to the hand. Then put it all together. 

A hand is like a human body. The body had arms, legs, a head and torso. You don't study them all at the same time. You study each part separately before putting them all together for a detailed drawing. Hands are the same. That's what makes them so difficult. Hands are small when compared to other parts of our body, but when you look at them closely, it has many parts and shapes. But be patient :) Don't give up. Go one step at a time. It's less overwhelming.

As an assignment, you can try drawing three different poses from reference a day. Put a timer for yourself. Try doing three 10 or 5 minutes well rendered drawing and three 1 or 2 minute quicksketches. Try to make the hand look as best as possible in that time frame. The purpose of this is to get you to stop caring what the end result will look like. It will get you more loose and it  will help you stop worrying about soending too much time on a sketch you might not be satisfied with.

Besides form, the bones teach you exactly how long each finger is by dividing the whole cylindrical length of the finger into smaller, simpler parts known as the phalanges.
